mcqs.q: Which liver function explains the bleeding tendency in cirrhosis?
mcqs.explain: The liver synthesises clotting factors; in cirrhosis their production falls, causing a bleeding tendency (prolonged PT/INR).

mcqs.q: Cirrhosis is defined pathologically as:
opts: Necrosis of liver cells followed by fibrosis and nodule formation
Fatty change that is fully reversible
A simple cyst in the liver
mcqs.explain: Cirrhosis is necrosis of hepatocytes followed by fibrosis and regenerative nodules, distorting architecture and impairing blood flow and function.

mcqs.q: Stage 1 (compensated) cirrhosis is characterised by:
opts: Being asymptomatic, often for 10–20 years, with near-normal life expectancy
mcqs.explain: Compensated cirrhosis is asymptomatic, can last 10–20 years with near-normal life expectancy; decompensation marks stage 2.

mcqs.q: Which is a classic systemic sign of chronic liver disease?
mcqs.explain: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, ascites, clubbing and Dupuytren's contracture are classic signs of chronic liver disease.

mcqs.q: Reddening of the palms in cirrhosis is termed:
mcqs.explain: Palmar erythema is reddening of the palms; Dupuytren's contracture is a separate fibrotic thickening of the palmar fascia.

mcqs.q: A LOW level of which protein indicates impaired liver synthesis?
mcqs.explain: Albumin is made by the liver, so a low albumin indicates impaired synthetic function; bilirubin and the enzymes rise rather than fall.

mcqs.q: A prolonged prothrombin time (PT) in liver disease reflects:
mcqs.explain: PT (10–14 s normally) is prolonged because the cirrhotic liver makes fewer clotting factors.

mcqs.q: An increased AST/ALT ratio is particularly suggestive of:
mcqs.explain: The AST/ALT ratio is usually increased in alcoholic hepatitis; ALP rises with bile-duct obstruction.

mcqs.q: Thrombocytopenia in cirrhosis is mainly due to:
mcqs.explain: Splenomegaly from portal hypertension sequesters platelets (hypersplenism), lowering the circulating count.

mcqs.q: The DEFINITIVE diagnosis of cirrhosis is made by:
mcqs.explain: Histological examination of a liver biopsy gives the definitive diagnosis; imaging and LFTs support it.

mcqs.q: A serum α-fetoprotein above 400 ng/mL suggests:
mcqs.explain: A markedly raised α-fetoprotein (>400 ng/mL) suggests hepatocellular carcinoma arising in a cirrhotic liver.

mcqs.q: Which investigation is both diagnostic AND therapeutic for oesophageal varices?
mcqs.explain: Endoscopy diagnoses and treats varices (e.g. banding) and portal hypertensive gastropathy; ultrasound assesses liver size/echogenicity.

mcqs.q: Intra-hepatic portal hypertension is most commonly caused by:
mcqs.explain: Intra-hepatic portal hypertension is due to architectural distortion (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis); pre-hepatic = portal vein thrombosis, post-hepatic = Budd-Chiari/right heart failure.

mcqs.q: Often the only clinical sign of portal hypertension is:
mcqs.explain: Portal hypertension is often asymptomatic, with splenomegaly the only sign until variceal bleeding, ascites or encephalopathy appear.

mcqs.q: Rupture of oesophageal varices typically presents as:
mcqs.explain: Ruptured gastro-oesophageal varices cause haematemesis (vomiting blood) or melaena (black stools).

mcqs.q: Spontaneous gingival bleeding and oral petechiae in cirrhosis result from:
mcqs.explain: Impaired vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors plus thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism) cause spontaneous gingival bleeding, ecchymoses and petechiae.

mcqs.q: Bilateral, painless parotid enlargement in a cirrhotic patient is called:
mcqs.explain: Sialadenosis — bilateral painless parotid hypertrophy — is a frequent finding in cirrhosis.

mcqs.q: Before invasive dental procedures in liver disease, the key screening tests are:
opts: CBC, AST/ALT, bleeding time and PT/INR
mcqs.explain: CBC with differential, AST/ALT, bleeding time, thrombin time and PT are screened before invasive procedures; abnormal results prompt physician referral.

mcqs.q: A patient with UNTREATED alcoholic liver disease needing an elective extraction should be:
opts: Referred to a physician first; elective outpatient care is not appropriate yet
mcqs.explain: An untreated alcoholic-liver-disease patient is not a candidate for elective outpatient dental care and should be medically managed first.

mcqs.q: The accepted thresholds for performing dental surgery in cirrhosis are about:
opts: Any INR if antibiotics are given
mcqs.explain: Surgery is generally acceptable with a maximum INR of 3.5 and a minimum platelet count of 50,000/mm³, with local haemostatic measures.

mcqs.q: Which local anaesthetic is PREFERRED in liver cirrhosis?
opts: Articaine (preferred over lidocaine), at normal doses but a lower maximum
mcqs.explain: LA is safe at normal doses (with a lower maximum); articaine is preferred to lidocaine in liver disease.

mcqs.q: Which analgesic approach is appropriate in cirrhosis?
mcqs.explain: Use reduced paracetamol (≤2 g/day short term) or codeine; avoid NSAIDs because of GI bleeding and renal risk.

mcqs.q: Which inhalational/sedative agent should be AVOIDED in liver disease?
mcqs.explain: Halothane is avoided as it can cause hepatitis; nitrous oxide and inhalation sedation are acceptable, and midazolam doses are reduced.

mcqs.q: To prevent hepatorenal syndrome (acute renal failure) when operating on a jaundiced patient, give:
opts: Nothing by mouth and no fluids
mcqs.explain: IV fluids, diuretics and mannitol help prevent acute renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome) in surgery on jaundiced patients.

mcqs.q: After a liver transplant, elective dental treatment should be:
mcqs.explain: No elective dental treatment for 3 months after transplant; routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended, and recall begins after 3 months.

mcqs.q: Which local measure helps control bleeding after extraction in a cirrhotic patient?
opts: Sutures, collagen sponge and tranexamic acid
mcqs.explain: Local haemostatics — sutures, collagen sponge, tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic) — control bleeding; FFP/vitamin K/platelets may also be needed.

saqs.q: List the main functions of the liver and link two to cirrhosis complications.
saqs.a: Metabolism/detox (glucose, drugs, bilirubin), synthesis (clotting factors, albumin, bile), storage/filtration. Failing clotting factors → bleeding; low albumin → ascites.

saqs.q: Define cirrhosis and distinguish compensated from decompensated disease.
saqs.a: Necrosis → fibrosis → nodule formation with loss of architecture. Compensated: asymptomatic, 10–20 years. Decompensated: onset of jaundice, ascites, bleeding, encephalopathy.

saqs.q: List the key liver function tests and what an abnormal result means.
Classify portal hypertension by site and give its presentation.
saqs.a: Pre-hepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intra-hepatic (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis), post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari, right heart failure). Presents with splenomegaly, variceal haematemesis/melaena, ascites, encephalopathy.

saqs.q: List the oral manifestations of liver cirrhosis.
saqs.a: Glossitis/loss of papillae, angular/labial cheilitis (candida), spontaneous gingival bleeding, petechiae, ecchymoses, sialadenosis (parotid enlargement), sweet musty breath, poor hygiene/caries.

saqs.q: State the bleeding-risk precautions for dental surgery in cirrhosis.
saqs.a: Screen with CBC/PT/INR; surgery needs INR ≤3.5 and platelets ≥50,000. Use local haemostatics, vitamin K, FFP, platelets or tranexamic acid; refer untreated alcoholic-liver patients to a physician.

saqs.q: Summarise safe drug/anaesthetic choices in cirrhosis.
saqs.a: LA safe (articaine preferred, lower maximum). Avoid NSAIDs, hepatotoxic drugs and halothane; use reduced paracetamol (≤2 g/day)/codeine; antibiotics (penicillin/amoxicillin/metronidazole) OK; reduce midazolam, prefer inhalation sedation.
